lines.text: Can you prove the Pythagorean theorem without any algebra? Let's do it with just four triangles.
Here's a right triangle. Its two short sides are a and b, and the long side is c.
The theorem says: a squared, plus b squared, equals c squared.
Make four copies of the triangle, and fit them into a big square, with sides a plus b.
Look at the empty space in the middle. It's a tilted square, with every side c. So its area is c squared.
Now slide the very same triangles into new spots, inside the very same square.
This time, the empty space is two squares. One is a squared, the other is b squared.
Same big square. Same four triangles. So the space that's left over must be the same, too.
And that means a squared plus b squared equals c squared. Proved, just by moving shapes!
Try it with three, four and five. Nine, plus sixteen, is twenty five.
See you in the next story!
